title: Big School Survey Shows More Preschoolers and More Suspensions
summary:
Every few years, the U.S. government runs a big survey called the Civil Rights Data Collection. It shows how students are treated in public schools. The newest one covers the 2023-24 school year. It includes about 49.7 million students in more than 97,000 schools.

Two researchers, Maithreyi Gopalan and Dan Losen, studied the data and shared what they found with NPR.

More young kids went to preschool. About 1.5 million children were in public preschool, 12% more than in 2021-22.

More students were suspended, or sent out of school as a punishment. Students missed over 14 million school days this way. Losen said many suspensions are for small problems, like being late. He said helping students can work better.

The survey counted teachers by race for the first time since the 1970s. Teachers are 75% white, 9% Black and 11% Latino.

The government chose not to share data it collected about nonbinary students.
why_it_matters: The survey helps make sure kids like you are treated fairly at school.

background_read: The U.S. government collects information from public schools to check that all students are treated fairly.
Laws say schools cannot treat students unfairly because of their race, whether they are a boy or a girl, or a disability.
The results help leaders see where students may need more help.
